newsitem.title: USA: Orange County D.A. disqualified in bankruptcy case.
newsitem.headline: Orange County D.A. disqualified in bankruptcy case.

text.p: A California appeals court on Friday disqualified Orange County's district attorney from prosecuting the county auditor-controller, Steven Lewis, on accusations stemming from the county's bankruptcy.
The state's Fourth District Court of Appeal in Santa Ana granted a request by Lewis to have the county district attorney and his office recused from his case.

The decision was yet another setback for Orange County District Attorney Michael Capizzi. Earlier this month, the California Supreme Court denied his request to revive misconduct charges against two county supervisors.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
In December 1995, a county grand jury accused Lewis, former county Supervisor Roger Stanton and current Board of Supervisors Chairman William Steiner of misconduct.
The grand jury alleged that Lewis failed to report report county cash-flow projections accurately, allowing the county to inflate the size of its tax-exempt borrowings.
Attorneys for Lewis argued that Capizzi had a conflict of interest and that their client would not receive a fair trial.
In the ruling Friday, the appeals court sided with Lewis.

"We hold there exists the appearance of a conflict so grave as to render it unlikely petitioner (Lewis) will receive fair treatment during the proceedings and order the motion to recuse be granted," the appeals court ruling said.
The court said the district attorney and his staff were "direct victims of the alleged conduct underlying the accusation" and that "the district attorney's own conduct may become an issue at trial."
An attorney for Lewis hailed the ruling.
"It (the ruling) gives Mr. Lewis the opportunity to have a fair trial," defense attorney Ellyn Garofalo said, adding that she has asked the appeals court to dismiss the case outright.
Maurice Evans, Orange County's chief assistant district attorney, said his office would review the ruling and consult with the state Attorney General's office.
"Sometime next week we'll make a decision about any action we may take regarding the opinion," he said.
The Lewis decision was a major blow to Orange County's district attorney, who lost another bankruptcy-related court battle earlier this month.
In addition to Lewis, the county grand jury had accused Stanton and Steiner of misconduct.

Prosecutors alleged the supervisors failed to oversee county finance officials and voted to issue bonds without making "adequate inquiries" into the need for the borrowings and whether the county could rapay them.
Last November, a state appeals court dismissed the accusations, saying that "something more than neglect" was needed to constitute misconduct.
On March 21, the California Supreme Court declined to reinstate the charges.
Wylie Aitken, Stanton's attorney, on Friday said the district attorney had finally come "to the end of the road."
"This whole chapter has now been brought to a close," Aitken said.
